profile.summary: John's Apocalypse is a prophetic and visionary message given to strengthen Christians pressured by opposition, persecution and superficial spiritual commitments. The book combines warning and comfort: it announces judgments against the enemies of Christ, reveals God's sovereign domination over history and points to the eternal hope of the faithful people. Its center is not to feed curiosity about future chronologies, but to show that the crucified and resurrected Lamb has already won and that the saints must persevere with fidelity to the end.
profile.setting: The work was probably written in the 1990s, although the possibility of a date in the 60s AD is also defended. John received the visions at Patmos, where he was as a political and religious prisoner. The historical scenario is that of increasing pressure on Christians in the Roman province of Asia: there was Jewish hostility against Jesus" followers and a strong demand for allegiance to the Roman emperor. In this context, the work encourages royal churches of western Turkey, linked to a geographical route that included the seven cities mentioned in chapters 2-3.

structure.label: Introduction and letters to the seven churches
structure.description: Presentation of the prophetic character of the book, initial greeting, vision of glorified Christ and direct messages to the churches of Asia.

structure.label: Throne of God and the Lamb
structure.description: Celestial Scenario that exalts the sovereign majesty of God and presents Jesus as the Lamb worthy of opening the book.

structure.label: The seals and trumpets
structure.description: Two series of judgments that reveal Christ's control over history, with intervals that show protection and witness to God's people.

structure.label: cosmic conflict and the forces of evil
structure.description: Symbolic views of the battle between good and evil, including the dragon, the beasts, and the contrast with the Lamb and his faithful.

structure.label: The seven bowls of anger
structure.description: Introduction liturgical followed by the last series of plagues, which intensifies the picture of divine judgment.

structure.label: The fall of Babylon and the outcome of the enemies of God
structure.description: Judgment of the great whore, fall of the evil powers, final defeat of the forces of evil, the devil and death.

structure.label: The new creation and the final invitation
structure.description: Vision of the new Jerusalem, the eternal hope of the people of God and the final call to come and await the coming of Christ.

themes: Victory of the Lamb crucified and risen
Divine judgment against evil and against those who resist Christ
Eternal hope, comfort and reward for God's people
readingKeys: Read the book as a prophetic vision full of images, not as a chronological manual of future events.
Notice how the series of seals, trumpets and bowls function as symbolic pictures of God's judgment and control.
Pay attention to the contrast between the powers of the world and the Lamb, and note how the book calls the church to perseverance and witness.
profile.cautions: The Apocalypse is a book especially difficult and interpreted in varied ways throughout history. The authorship is traditionally attributed to the apostle John, but the text identifies itself only as "John"; identification with the apostle is the most common position in the ancient church, although the source emphasizes that the issue is treated in a traditional way and not as absolute proof. The date is also not consensual: many defend the end of Domitian's reign, but some propose the 60s. As an apocalyptic work, it uses symbolic language, images and numbers in order to communicate a spiritual message, and should not be read as if each view had to be tightly embedded in a literal and systematic sequence.

dossier.narratedEra: The setting narrated in Revelation lies at the end of the 1st century, within the world of the churches of the Roman province of Asia (western present-day Turkey), with social, religious and possibly persecutory pressure on Christians. The visions deal with the Roman empire, its symbols of power, and the opposition between the dominion of Christ and the structures of the world.
dossier.compositionEra: The given notes indicate as the most likely date of composition the final years of Domitian's reign (approx. A.D. 94-96), or immediately after (AD 96-99); they also recognize an alternative composition proposal in the 1960s, in the context of Nero and persecution of the church. The traditional authorship is attributed to John, identified in the ancient church as the apostle John. The sources also record the mention of John's exile in Patmos as the occasion of the reception of visions.

politics.title: Imperial pressure and allegiance to the emperor
politics.detail: Tyndale's introduction states that Rome required absolute allegiance to the emperor and that, at least in the pro-Roman province of Asia, anyone who refused to worship the emperor could face severe persecution. This helps to read the confessions of Jesus as Lord in direct contrast to imperial language.
politics.readingImpact: The assertion that Jesus is the true sovereign gains political strength: Christian fidelity is not only religious, but also a resistance to Caesar's absolute pretense.

politics.title: Tense relation between Jews and Christians after Jamnia
politics.detail: Tyndale reports that in the 1990s, Jews would have condemned Christianity in their assemblies of Jamnia (AD 70-85) and reported Christians to the Roman authorities as religious dissidents without legal protection. The note is presented as a background for the hostility faced by readers.
politics.readingImpact: Letters to churches and references to religious opposition should be read in the light of exclusion and denunciation, not social neutrality.

politics.title: Rome as power symbolized by Babylon
politics.detail: Tyndale's note on Revelation 17 identifies Babylon as a code for Rome, and the introduction associates the great city with the Roman world. This is not presented as purely geographical detail, but as a symbolic language of criticism of imperial power.
politics.readingImpact: Claims against Babylon should be read as an attack on the Roman oppressive order and its alleged security, and not just as a description of an isolated city.

politics.title: The Osres of Revelation 17 and the Roman Emperors
politics.detail: Tyndale's introduction suggests that the eight kings of Revelation 17:7-11 may refer to the eight Roman emperors from Augustus to Domitian. The source presents this as an interpretative possibility, not as a historical certainty.
politics.readingImpact: The reader is led to perceive the vision as a commentary on imperial successions and the transience of the power of Rome.

politics.title: John as a political and religious prisoner in Patmos
politics.detail: Tyndale describes John as imprisoned and exiled at Patmos, a rocky island used as a Roman prison off the western coast of Asia Minor, near Ephesus. The note links this exile to the prophetic announcement received.
politics.readingImpact: Revelation is born in the context of imperial coercion; therefore, the book speaks of hope for oppressed people, not abstract theory.

customs.title: Christian Meeting on the Lord's Day
customs.detail: Tyndale notes that in the Roman world, expressions linked to the Lord's Day could refer to celebrations in honor of Caesar, but Christians applied it to the weekly cult in memory of Jesus" resurrection. The same note says that Christians, excluded from the synagogues in the time of Revelation, met on the first day of the week.
customs.readingImpact: Prophetic instruction is received amidst distinct cult practices and a Christian identity already separated from the synagogue environment.

customs.title: Synagogues, exclusion and community identity
customs.detail: The introduction states that in the period of Revelation, Christians were excluded from the synagogues. This helps to understand the book's self-awareness as a word for marginalized and distinct communities from its ancient religious contexts.
customs.readingImpact: The letters and exhortations to the churches sound as a formation of identity and perseverance in a situation of exclusion.

customs.title: Burlap/bag as a sign of grief or repentance
customs.detail: In Revelation 11:3, Tyndale explains that bagwear was a symbol of grief or repentance. This observation is part of the image of the two testimonies crying out in the midst of the judgment announced.
customs.readingImpact: The garment indicates that the prophetic ministry is marked by call to repentance, not by worldly triumph.

customs.title: Public display of bodies as dishonor
customs.detail: Commenting on Revelation 11:8-9, Tyndale says that leaving bodies on public display was a dishonor form, and notes that the Roman custom was to leave bodies hanging after crucifixion. The scene reinforces the humiliation of the dead testimonies.
customs.readingImpact: Reading perceives the symbolic violence of persecution: it is not only about death, but of public shame and an attempt to silence the message.

customs.title: Work of scribes and preservation of the text
customs.detail: In Revelation 22:18-19, Tyndale notes that at the time of writing scribes sometimes changed books to adjust the content to their own ideas. The note defends the integrity of the text and the need for authenticity in the transmission.
customs.readingImpact: The closing of the book includes a textual and communitarian warning: the church must receive the prophecy as it was given, without manipulation.

language.title: Apocalypse as revelation/apocalyptic
language.detail: The notes highlight the Greek term apokalupsis as an indication of the visionary character of the book. The language of Revelation is described as made of symbols, numbers and images, more than linear reasoning.
language.readingImpact: The reader should think of frames and visions, not in rigid sequence of events; this avoids forcing a systematization that gender does not require.

language.title: Use of "Babylon" as code for Rome
language.detail: Tyndale explicitly states that Babylon functions as a code for Rome in Revelation 17. The coded language is presented as a characteristic of apocalyptic writings in pressure times.
language.readingImpact: The criticism of power is veiled to those from outside, but clear to the believing readers; the city is not only literal, but a symbol of a hostile order to God.

language.title: Seven as a symbol of completeness and perfection
language.detail: The notes in 1:4-8 and 1:12-20 observe that the seven marks the fullness: seven churches, seven spirits (understood as the Holy Spirit in their perfection), seven candlesticks and seven stars. The number points to totality and integrity, not just literal count.
language.readingImpact: The vision broadens the scope: the recipient churches represent the whole church, and the presence of the Spirit and Christ encompasses the whole reality of the community.

language.title: Imaging contrast between lion and lamb
language.detail: Tyndale reads Revelation 5 as the presentation of Jesus as a lion and lamb at the same time, uniting power and sacrifice. This combination is central to the way the book depicts divine victory.
language.readingImpact: The authority of Christ is interpreted not by brute force, but by the cross and resurrection; this shapes the ethics of faithful suffering.

language.title: Mouth-sword, flaminged eyes and court images
language.detail: In Revelation 1:14-16, Tyndale explains images such as eyes of fire, bronze feet and sword that comes out of the mouth as signs of discernment, firmness, and effective judgment. The mouth that wields sword emphasizes that the word of Christ judges.
language.readingImpact: The language is not decorative: it teaches that Christ's speech is active, penetrating and judging, and that his presence already evaluates the church.

timeline.title: Possible date of composition in the years 90 AD.
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Revelation was probably written in the 1990s, during or after the reign of Domitian. The note presents this as the main hypothesis.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading is situated in the scene of the maturation of persecution and sharper confrontation with the imperial cult.

timeline.title: Alternative composition in the 60s AD.
timeline.detail: The same notes admit the possibility of composition in the 1960s, when Nero pursued the church and killed Christians. The source does not solve the debate, only records it.
timeline.readingImpact: The interpreter must be cautious in relating the visions to a unique historical moment, because the date affects the way the imperial backdrop is read.

timeline.title: Jamnia and the Jewish-Christian withdrawal
timeline.detail: Tyndale places the condemnation of Christianity in Jamnia between AD 70 and 85. This is part of the background for the exclusion and denunciation of Christians.
timeline.readingImpact: The hostility in Revelation comes not only from Rome; there is also a religious rupture with post-70 Judaism, which intensifies pressure on readers.

timeline.title: Destruction of Jerusalem Temple in AD 70
timeline.detail: In Revelation 11:1, Tyndale's note mentions the destruction of the Temple by the Romans in A.D. 70 and compares the measurement of the temple with visions of Ezekiel. This is used as a backdrop for the symbolism of measuring.
timeline.readingImpact: The temple scene should be read as a language of care and distinction of God's people, not simply as an architectural report.

timeline.title: "Three years and a half" as a time of persecution
timeline.detail: In Revelation 11:2-3, Tyndale plays 42 months and 1,260 days as three and a half years, a broken "sixth." The expression is used when persecution is evident and evil seems to dominate.
timeline.readingImpact: The short and incomplete time communicates limitation of oppressive power; suffering has a marked duration and under the control of God.

timeline.title: Patmos as the place of sending the visions
timeline.detail: The notes describe John receiving the visions on Patmos, an island used as Roman prison, and sending the message to the churches of the province of Asia. The path of the letters is thought of as a geographical route between seven cities.
timeline.readingImpact: The circulation of the book by royal churches reinforces its pastoral and public function, not only private or mystical.

investigation: The sources converge in reading Revelation as a message of consolation and warning to churches under pressure, but differ or remain open as to the exact date of composition.
The traditional joanine authorship is affirmed in the notes, but the source also recognizes that many scholars discuss the date and context without completely closing the picture.
Symbolic reading is central: Babylon, beasts, numbers and times are treated as apocalyptic language, but some historical identifications are presented only as possibilities.
The section on the temple in Revelation 11 combines image of Ezekiel, memory of the destroyed temple and pastoral interpretation; this requires caution not to turn symbol into literal chronology.

Matthew Henry's notes emphasize the authoriality and value of the book, while Tyndale offers more contextual details and literary explanations; both are confessional and do not claim independent historical proof.

There is no in the sources a broad inventory of economics, food or domestic organization in Revelation; the customs documented here are those explicitly linked to the notes on worship, mourning, persecution, exile and textual transmission.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the notes provided and, therefore, is selective: it privileges what the sources really discuss and avoids filling gaps with external knowledge. Some statements are explicitly presented as interpretations of the notes, especially the relations with Domitian, Nero, the eight kings, Babylon, and the symbolic extension of the seven churches. The coverage of daily customs is limited because the sources deal mainly with worship, persecution, exile, grief, honor/deson and preservation of the text, not of a broad ethnography of daily life. There is also legitimate internal tension between historical and symbolic readings, and the dossier seeks to register it without solving it beyond what the notes authorize.
